neutral_facts.value: The accused was implicated in a case involving the siphoning of public funds amounting to approximately Rs.370 crores. The case involved allegations of misappropriation of government funds through the establishment of a corporation and subsequent agreements with corporate entities. The accused was alleged to have unilaterally appointed individuals as MD and CEO without cabinet approval, leading to the approval of a budget for the project. The investigation revealed discrepancies in the project's financial management, including the use of shell companies and fake invoices. The accused was added as an accused in the FIR after an initial investigation into the matter. The case involved allegations of criminal breach of trust and fraud, with the accused being charged under multiple sections of the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act. The trial court remanded the accused to judicial custody, and the High Court dismissed the petition seeking quashing of the FIR and the remand order.

procedural_irregularity.value: Absence of prior approval under s.17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988

quotes.text: Plea of the appellant inter alia that the absence of prior approval as mandated by s.17A vitiated the conduct of enquiry or inquiry or investigation

The appellant applied before the High Court on 12.09.2023 for quashing the F.I.R. in Crime No. 29 of 2021 implicating him, invoking the jurisdiction of the Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (1973 Code). The legality of the remand order dated 10.09.2023 was also challenged in the same petition before the High Court. The appellant’s plea was rejected and his petition was dismissed on 22.09.2023 by a learned Single Judge.
The present appeal is against this judgment of dismissal of the said petition.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant was the mastermind behind the diversion of public funds, having unilaterally appointed officials and approved the cost estimation with criminal intent. The State also contended that the FIR and remand order were valid and that the Special Court had jurisdiction to proceed against the appellant for the alleged offences under the IPC and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

quotes.text: The State’s case that requirement of contribution of the two corporate entities was ignored and the final memorandum of agreement only entailed outflow of Rs.330/- crores from the State to Design Tech.
It is the State’s case that these companies were shell/defunct companies and they had issued invoices without providing any services and that they were used as vehicles for diverting funds.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the initiation of proceedings against the appellant was invalid due to non-compliance with Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, which requires prior approval from the appropriate authority for any enquiry, inquiry, or investigation into offences committed by a public servant. They also contended that the entire proceeding would collapse if the allegations under the 1988 Act were found to be invalid.

quotes.text: Plea of the appellant inter alia that the absence of prior approval as mandated by s.17A vitiated the conduct of enquiry or inquiry or investigation

The appellant argued that if the initial action was not in consonance with law, all subsequent and consequential proceedings would fall and once offences under the PC Act were effaced from existence, the custody of the appellant pursuant to the orders passed by the Special Court was without any sanction of law

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the legislative intent of the Prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 2018 was to make Section 17A applicable only to new offences and not to those existing prior to the amendment. The Court also emphasized that the right of the investigating agency to investigate offences committed before the amendment is not affected by the repeal of the old provisions.

quotes.text: It is required to be presumed that the intention of the legislature was to make Section 17A applicable only to the new offences as amended by Amendment Act, 2018 and not to the offences which existed prior to the coming into force of the Amendment Act 2018.

The well-known and well accepted rule of interpretation of statute is that the courts should take into consideration the other provisions of the Act also while interpreting a particular provision, and should avoid such interpretation as would lead to an anomalous situation or to frustration of the object of the Act.
